title: Armor the planes where there are no holes
summary: Survivorship bias: drawing conclusions only from the cases that made it through. The WWII bomber story is the classic example — and the same trap hides in success stories.
evidenceNote: Abraham Wald's WWII analysis is real, but the popular version is simplified: his reports were mathematical estimates, and the well-known 'red dots' plane diagram is a modern illustration.

scenes.text: Bombers return riddled with bullet holes. Where should you add armor?
In WWII, statistician Abraham Wald studied aircraft damage. The key point: you only see the planes that made it back.
Holes on returning planes show where a plane can be hit and still survive. The lost planes were hit elsewhere.

scenes.reveal: Wald's real work was mathematical estimates — the famous diagram came much later.

scenes.text: The same trap appears in business.
